title: Recognising and managing snuffles in rabbits
subtitle: Snuffles is a chronic bacterial infection, not a cold. Most rabbits carry it; few ever show symptoms.
excerpt: Snuffles is a broad term for upper respiratory infection in rabbits, most commonly caused by Pasteurella multocida. A rabbit with a thick nasal discharge, wet matted fur on the inside of its forepaws, and frequent sneezing is showing the classic presentation. Mild cases can be managed with supportive care; persistent cases need a vet.
sourceNotes: RSPCA rabbit health guidance. British Rabbit Council health notes, Pasteurella section. Judith Bell, Rabbits (Crowood Animal Series, 2012), chapter on respiratory disease. DEFRA animal health advisory material.

glossaryTerms.definition: Pasteurella multocida, a bacterium carried by most domestic rabbits without causing illness. Stress, cold, damp conditions, or a weakened immune system can trigger active infection.
Mucus from the nostrils. In rabbits with snuffles it ranges from clear and watery in early stages to thick white or yellowish as infection becomes established.

content.text: Snuffles is caused by
Pasteurella

bacteria, which most rabbits carry without ever showing signs. The infection activates when conditions stress the animal: overcrowding, poor ventilation, damp bedding, or a period of illness. Once established, snuffles is rarely curable but can be managed for a good quality of life.
Recognising the signs
Thick
nasal discharge
, white, cream, or pale yellow mucus around the nostrils.
Wet, matted fur on the inside of the front legs where the rabbit has been wiping its nose.
Frequent sneezing, sometimes in clusters.
In established cases: runny eyes, head tilt (if infection reaches the inner ear), or changes in breathing sounds.
Supportive care for mild cases
A rabbit with mild snuffles, clear discharge, and otherwise normal behaviour may not need antibiotics. Focus on removing the environmental triggers.
Improve ventilation in the hutch. Snuffles flares in damp, poorly aired spaces. The hutch should have moving air without being draughty.
Replace bedding daily or every other day. Wet straw generates ammonia fumes that irritate already inflamed nasal passages.
Clean the nostrils and the inside of the front legs with a cotton pad dampened with saline solution. Remove crusted discharge gently.
Ensure unlimited hay access. A rabbit that stops eating loses condition quickly and the infection progresses.
When to see a vet
Discharge becomes thick and purulent after 5-7 days of improved conditions.
The rabbit stops eating or drinking.
Head tilt appears, or the rabbit loses balance.
Breathing becomes laboured or audible at rest.

Antibiotics are used for established snuffles. Enrofloxacin and trimethoprim-sulphonamide are typical choices. The bacterium can be resistant, so sensitivity testing helps find the best drug. Long-term use is sometimes needed. Discuss this with your vet, weighing the rabbit's quality of life.
Preventing spread to other rabbits

Pasteurella passes by direct contact, grooming, and shared water. A rabbit showing active signs should be separated from others until symptoms resolve. Clean and disinfect shared equipment. Do not introduce new rabbits until the affected animal is symptom-free for at least four weeks.
